description: The two statement tools: query runs reads and write runs writes. A statement of the other kind denies as tool, naming the one that runs it, once scope has passed: a read-only caller's write is a scope denial, not a pointer to a tool it doesn't have. A case without `accepts` runs either kind, as the rest of the corpus does.

cases.name: a read through query runs read-only
a write through query is refused, naming the write tool
cases.sql: UPDATE users SET name = 'x' WHERE id = 1

expect.reason_includes: a write (UPDATE) and the query tool runs reads only

cases.name: SELECT INTO creates a table, so query refuses it
a schema change through query is refused the same way
a write through write follows the policy
cases.sql: UPDATE users SET name = 'x' WHERE id = 1

cases.name: a held class still holds through write
cases.sql: UPDATE users SET name = 'x' WHERE id = 1

cases.name: a read through write is refused, naming the query tool

expect.reason_includes: a read and the write tool runs writes only

cases.name: scope is checked before the tool: a read-only caller's write through query is refused as read-only
a write hidden in a WITH query is classified as a read, so query reaches the hidden-write rule
cases.sql: WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM logs WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id) SELECT id FROM gone

cases.name: a write hidden in a WITH query, sent to write, is a hidden write, not 'a read'
cases.sql: WITH gone AS (DELETE FROM logs WHERE id = 1 RETURNING id) SELECT id FROM gone

cases.name: a read that wouldn't run anyway, sent to write, gets its real reason
without accepts, either kind runs
cases.sql: UPDATE users SET name = 'x' WHERE id = 1
